1170.title: When I dance, I dance
1170.hook: when I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep (Essays 3.13)
1170.carry: be wholly in what you do; drift, return
1170.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often quote his line from Of experience, when I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep, as a picture of giving full attention to ordinary acts.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was plague years: Montaigne learning steadiness from people who'd read none of his books. Your line was the peasants' calm. A new week starts now.

Dinner is on the table, the phone is next to the plate, the news murmurs in the other room, and half your mind is already in tomorrow's meeting. Afterward, you could hardly say what you ate. Montaigne, in the last essay of his book, called Of experience, describes another way of being at the table, on the dance floor, in bed at night. The sentence could hardly be plainer: when I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep.
screen: `DINNER, PHONE, NEWS, TOMORROW.` → `WHAT DID YOU EAT?` → `WHEN I DANCE, I DANCE.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. It sounds almost too obvious. Of course when you dance, you dance. But Montaigne means it as a discipline: when he does a thing, he tries to be wholly in it, not half there and half somewhere else. Second, the orchard. He doesn't pretend to be perfect at it. Walking alone in a beautiful orchard, he says, his thoughts sometimes drift to far-away matters for part of the time. For the other part, he brings them back: to the walk, the orchard, the sweetness of being alone there, and to himself. Drift, and return. That's the whole skill. Third, the body's ordinary work. Nature, he says, has made the actions it requires of us pleasant: eating, sleeping, resting. To rush them, or look down on them as beneath a serious mind, misses something nature gave on purpose. He's suspicious of people who treat a good meal as a waste of time. Fourth, the great men. Even generals and rulers he admired, he points out, found time for ordinary pleasures in the middle of great affairs. Being wholly present wasn't a distraction from serious life; it was part of living it well. Washing a cup, hugging a child at the door: when you wash, wash. When you hug, hug.
screen: `DO ONE THING WHOLLY.` · `DRIFT, THEN COME BACK.` · `NATURE MADE NEEDS PLEASANT.` · `PRESENT IN GREAT AFFAIRS TOO.` · then, large: `WHEN I DANCE, I DANCE.`

segments.voice: When you breathe in, breathe in; when you breathe out, breathe out. Your mind will wander, the way Montaigne's did in the orchard, and when you notice, don't scold it: bring it back to the breath, the chair, this room, yourself. Drift and return, as many times as it takes.
When I dance. Montaigne's short rule for being wholly in what you're doing, and coming back when you drift. Today's word.
Your line: be wholly in what you do; drift, then return. When the mind wanders off, the orchard is still there to come back to. I'll be here tomorrow.

1171.title: Our own bottom
1171.hook: on the highest throne in the world, we still sit on our own bottom (Essays 3.13)
1171.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often quote his line that even on the highest throne we sit on our own bottom as a cheerful check on pride and a reminder that every life is lived in an ordinary body.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was when I dance: be wholly in what you're doing, and come back when you drift. Your line was when I dance, I dance.

A king climbs the steps to his throne. Velvet, gold, a crowd holding its breath. He turns, gathers his robes, and sits down. On what, exactly? Near the very end of Of experience, Montaigne answers with a joke. It's no use climbing up on stilts, he says, because on stilts we still have to walk with our own legs. And on the highest throne in the world, we are still sitting on our own bottom.
screen: `A KING CLIMBS TO HIS THRONE.` → `ON STILTS, OUR OWN LEGS.` → `ON THE THRONE, OUR OWN BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: First, the joke. It's a little rude, and that's the point. A throne is the grandest seat there is, and the body on it is as ordinary as anyone's. The laugh punctures the idea that rank, title or achievement lifts a person out of being human. Second, the stilts. Stilts are anything we use to seem taller: a job title, a following, an expensive coat, being right in an argument. Fine, climb up. You're still walking on your own legs, with their aches and limits. Nothing you stand on changes what you're standing with. Third, angels and beasts. In the same closing pages he warns about people who want to rise above the human, to escape being a person altogether. Instead of turning into angels, he says, they turn into beasts. He's wary of any striving, however lofty, that despises the body and ordinary life. Readers differ on how far to take this: some hear a gentle check on pride, others a reminder that the spiritual life is lived in a body, at a table, among people. Fourth, the laugh. Not with contempt; with relief. The pressure to be more than human is heavy, and Montaigne sets it down with one cheerful, slightly rude sentence. Whether you feel very important or very small, the line works both ways. Everyone you meet is sitting on the same thing.

1172.title: Haven't you lived?
1172.hook: "I've done nothing today." What, haven't you lived? (Essays 3.13)
1172.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often return to this passage from Of experience as a counterweight to measuring a day only by what got finished; some keep it as a short line to say at night.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was our own bottom: on the highest throne, Montaigne says, we still sit on our own bottom. Your line was my own bottom.

Ten-forty at night. The list on the fridge has the same five items it had at breakfast. The inbox is still full. And there's a sentence people say at that hour, out loud or under their breath: I did nothing today. Montaigne heard it too, and wrote it down in the essay called Of experience. He answered with a question so short it almost sounds rude. What, haven't you lived? He doesn't ask what got finished. He asks something stranger.
screen: `THE SAME FIVE ITEMS ON THE LIST.` → `I DID NOTHING TODAY.` → `WHAT, HAVEN'T YOU LIVED?`

segments.voice: First, the complaint. Montaigne calls us great fools, himself included. We say of someone, he spent his life in idleness. We say of ourselves, I've done nothing today. Second, his answer. Haven't you lived? Living isn't a gap between the real tasks, he says. It's the basic work, and the most excellent of all your occupations. Third, the excuse he hears next. If only I'd been given great affairs, people say, I'd have shown what I could do. Montaigne turns it around. Have you known how to think about your life and manage it? Then you've done the greatest work there is. Our job is to compose our character, not to compose books. The great and glorious masterpiece is to live fittingly. Everything else, ruling, piling up money, building, he calls little add-ons and props at most. And notice who's saying it: a man composing a book at that very moment. He isn't against work. He's against the ledger that only counts the work. Fourth, a plain week. You ate a meal. You talked someone through a bad hour. You noticed the light on the wall at four o'clock. You were tired, and patient anyway. None of that goes on the list on the fridge. In Montaigne's book, it's the masterpiece.

segments.voice: Go back through today, or yesterday if it's early, not by tasks but by moments: somewhere you woke, something you ate, a voice you heard, a moment you were kind or tried to be. Don't grade any of them. Set each one down like a coin on a table, and let the pile be what it is.

1173.title: Of experience
1173.hook: the book's last essay: know yourself through ordinary life (Essays 3.13)
1173.howItsDone: Readers often treat Of experience as the place where Montaigne's book gathers itself: he turns from theories and laws to what his own body, moods and mistakes have taught him.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was haven't you lived? It's Montaigne's answer to I've done nothing today. Your line was haven't I lived.

Some kitchens have a cook who never measures. A pinch of this, a splash of that, and somehow it comes out right. Ask for the recipe and you get a shrug: you just get a feel for it. No classroom taught that cook; ordinary dinners did. Montaigne ends his whole book with an essay built on that kind of knowing, called Of experience. Where do we really learn who we are? Not in the library, he says. In the kitchen, the sickbed, the bad temper, the night's sleep.
screen: `THE COOK WHO NEVER MEASURES.` → `A THOUSAND ORDINARY DINNERS.` → `THE LAST ESSAY: OF EXPERIENCE.`

segments.voice: First, where it starts. The desire to know is natural to us, Montaigne says, and we try every road to it. When reason isn't enough, we turn to experience. Then he shows how slippery reason gets: laws pile up and still can't fit every case, because life keeps producing new ones. Second, his turn inward. He studies himself, he says, more than any other subject. That is his metaphysics and his physics. It isn't a boast; he's simply the one case he can watch up close, every day. Third, what he learns. Remember how far your last anger carried you, he says, and you'll see its ugliness better than in any book of philosophy. Remember how often you were sure and wrong, and you'll trust the next certainty less. His teachers are his own illnesses, moods and mistakes, looked at honestly. Fourth, where it ends. The finest lives, he says, fit the ordinary human pattern, without miracles and without extravagance. And he closes the book not with a grand theory but with a wish for a healthy old age, borrowed from the Roman poet Horace. From the hunger to know everything, down to the plain lessons of one ordinary life: the cook's way of knowing, turned on the self.
screen: `WHEN REASON FAILS, EXPERIENCE.` · `I STUDY MYSELF.` · `REMEMBER YOUR LAST ANGER.` · `THE ORDINARY HUMAN PATTERN.` · then, large: `ORDINARY LESSONS.`

1174.title: The daughters
1174.hook: Montaigne lost five of six daughters in infancy and wrote little of it, which readers still wonder about
1174.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often pause at his one passing remark about losing children in infancy and read it in more than one way: as an honest report, or as grief held back from the page.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was of experience: the last essay, where Montaigne learns most from his own plain life. Your line was ordinary lessons.

Here is a man who tells you about his kidney stones, his digestion, his bad memory, how he likes his meat cooked and how long he likes to sleep. Nothing seems too small or too private for his book. Then, in one sentence, tucked inside an argument about something else, he mentions that some of his children died as babies. One sentence, and he moves on. Readers have stopped at that sentence for a long time and asked what's underneath it.
screen: `KIDNEY STONES, MEAT, MEMORY.` → `ONE SENTENCE ABOUT HIS CHILDREN.` → `THEN HE MOVES ON.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. In an early essay, Montaigne argues that much of what hurts us hurts because of the opinion we hold about it. As an example, he says he has lost two or three children while they were still nursing, not without regret, but without great grief. That's all. Second, what sits around it. The same writer gave a whole essay to his friend Étienne de La Boétie, and to losing him. Asked why he loved him, Montaigne says it could only be answered: because it was he, because it was I. He could write grief, openly and at length. Here he doesn't. Third, how readers take the silence. Some take him at his word: an honest report, from a time and place that spoke of such losses differently. Some hear a man using his own argument as armor, saying the calm thing because the true thing was too heavy for the page. Some notice he doesn't give the number exactly, two or three, and sit with that. Nobody can open the inside of another person's grief, and Montaigne doesn't open this one for us. Fourth, outside the book. The man next to you on the train, the coworker who laughs easily, the grandmother who never mentions the brother she lost. Some grief gets whole pages; some gets one sentence and a closed door. Both are real. The quiet kind asks for gentler eyes. And if a grief of your own grows too heavy, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US you can call or text 988, and wherever you are, local emergency help is there.

1175.title: The wars
1175.hook: France's religious wars raged around his tower, and he talked peace to both sides
1175.howItsDone: Montaigne describes keeping his house unguarded during France's civil wars and dealing openly with men on both sides, telling each what he would tell the other.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the daughters: one passing sentence that readers still wonder about. Your line was hidden grief.

A country house in France. Outside, armed bands from two sides of a civil war over religion ride the roads. Neighbors bar their gates, hire guards, and sleep badly. One house leaves its gate open. Inside, in a tower, a man is writing a book about himself. He belongs to one of the two churches and doesn't hide it. And men on both sides use him to carry word between them. Today, how Montaigne lived in the middle of a war about faith.
screen: `A CIVIL WAR OVER RELIGION.` → `ONE GATE LEFT OPEN.` → `WORD CARRIED BETWEEN THEM.`

segments.voice: First, the open gate. While others fortified their homes, Montaigne writes, he kept his unguarded, with only a porter at the door, more for old custom and ceremony than for defense. A guarded house, he reasons, invites attack, because it looks like a prize. His stayed open, and he says it was spared. Second, how he talked. In the essay Of the useful and the honest, he describes going between great men on opposite sides. He tells each plainly what he'd tell the other, and doesn't pretend to belong to the side he doesn't. Because he wasn't playing a game, people trusted him with their real thoughts. Third, his candle. He'd gladly carry a candle to Saint Michael, he says, and another to his dragon. It's a joke with an edge, told against himself: he'll follow his own side even to the fire, but not into it if he can help it. Fourth, the cost. In a later essay he admits moderation got him beaten from every side: one camp took him for the enemy, and the other camp did the same. Talking to both often makes both suspicious. He did it anyway, out loud, in his own name. The wars near us are smaller: two siblings, two friends who stopped speaking. His way isn't pretending they agree. It's keeping the gate open and saying the same true thing in both rooms.

1176.title: A Catholic doubter
1176.hook: he remained Catholic and died during Mass in 1592, while doubting nearly everything else
1176.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne differ on how to hold his doubt and his Catholic faith together: some read him as a sincere believer who thought reason could not reach God, others read the faith as a cover, and some leave the question open.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the wars: Montaigne kept his gate open and said the same plain words to both sides. Your line was talk to both.

A pair of scales, two pans hanging level. Montaigne took that image as his emblem, he says, with a short question beside it: what do I know? The same man submitted his writing to the judgment of the Church he was born in. He put the doubt and the faith in the same book, and hid neither one. Readers still argue about him, and about what that question left room for.
screen: `A PAIR OF BALANCED SCALES.` → `WHAT DO I KNOW?` → `AND STILL IN HIS CHURCH.`

segments.voice: First, the doubt. In the Apology for Raymond Sebond, Montaigne takes apart human confidence piece by piece. Our senses fool us. Our reason argues both sides of anything. Animals may know things we don't. Even the skeptics' own claim, I doubt, says too much, he thinks, because it sounds sure of itself. So he turns it into a question: what do I know? Second, the faith. In the essay Of prayers, he says he puts his thoughts forward as things to be explored, not truths to be believed, and submits them to the Church he was born in. He'd gladly see Christians use the Lord's Prayer at every turn. Third, how he holds them together, and here readers differ. Some read a sincere Catholic who thinks reason is too weak to reach God, so faith must come as a gift, not a proof. Some read the faith as a careful cover for a deeper doubt. Some say we simply can't see inside him, which would suit him well. Fourth, the end. Tradition says Montaigne died while Mass was being said in his room: the doubter, at the end, inside the rite of his church. Whatever you make of him, he didn't think faith and doubt had to evict each other. A scale doesn't need one pan empty to hang level.
screen: `OUR SENSES AND REASON FOOL US.` · `SUBMITTED TO THE CHURCH.` · `SINCERE, OR A COVER?` · `MASS SAID IN HIS ROOM.` · then, large: `FAITH AND DOUBT.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open, one on each knee, like the two pans of a scale. In one, place something you trust, whatever that is for you: a person, a practice, a belief, the sun coming up; in the other, a question you can't answer. Don't let either hand win; just feel the weight of both.
